snip.t: A common language so clinicians, patients, families and services mean the same thing by "schizophrenia" or "depression".
To guide treatment: the diagnosis points to evidence-based options (for example lithium for bipolar disorder, SSRIs plus CBT for depression).
Pressured speech (mania); poverty of speech and mutism (depression, schizophrenia); slow, monotonous (depression); dysarthria or slurring (neurological, intoxication).
Seen in: Schizophrenia, mania, psychotic depression, delirium — Schizophrenia, delirium, substance use, epilepsy — Delirium, anxiety, fatigue; can be normal
Anhedonia: Loss of interest or pleasure in previously enjoyable activities; a core feature of major depression and negative symptoms.
Anergia: Lack of energy or physical drive; commonly seen in depression and negative symptom clusters.
Euthymic: Normal, stable mood without significant elevation or depression.
The monoamine hypothesis says depression involves low serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine function.

qs.q: A postoperative patient develops a sudden drop in consciousness level and shallow breathing after receiving a dose of intravenous morphine for severe pain. Which component of the ABCDE assessment directly targets this respiratory depression?
o: Circulation assessment by checking capillary refill and peripheral pulses
Breathing assessment by checking respiratory rate and oxygen saturation
Disability assessment by measuring bedside capillary blood glucose
Exposure assessment by thoroughly checking the surgical wound and drains
qs.e: Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and opioid-induced respiratory depression are evaluated under the breathing component of the ABCDE survey. Although consciousness is checked in disability, the respiratory mechanics and gas exchange are breathing parameters.
qs.s: Postoperative Care and Assessment of the Surgical Patient: MCQs

qs.q: When implementing multimodal analgesia for moderate-to-severe pain in a postoperative patient, which group of drugs requires close monitoring for sedation, respiratory depression, and constipation?
o: Regular intravenous paracetamol infusions
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Topical local anaesthetic patches
Systemic opioid analgesics
qs.e: Opioids are used for moderate-to-severe pain with specific monitoring for sedation, respiratory depression, nausea, constipation, and urinary retention. Paracetamol and NSAIDs do not typically cause significant respiratory depression.

qs.q: A student analyzing a newly erupted maxillary first premolar observes a distinct depression on the mesial root surface. Which anatomical structure is this feature most closely associated with?
o: The furcation entrance pathway
The central occlusal sulcus area
The cervical enamel projection
The developmental root concavity
The supplemental marginal groove
qs.e: The mesial root surface of the maxillary first premolar characteristically features a developmental longitudinal concavity extending from the cervical line to the bifurcation.

qs.q: A histological examination of a fetal heart reveals a depression in the interatrial septum where the foramen ovale was. What is the name of this anatomical remnant?
o: The sinus venarum and its smooth lining
The foramen primum and its closed valve
The fossa ovalis and its fibrous rim
The coronary sinus and its orifice
The membranous septum and its fibrous tissue
qs.e: The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the foramen ovale.

qs.q: A patient with depression is prescribed fluoxetine. Which pharmacodynamic mechanism is primarily responsible for its antidepressant effect?
o: Prevents serotonin reabsorption at neuronal synaptic clefts.
Reduces activity of the monoamine oxidase enzyme.
Blocks dopamine receptors located in the central nervous system.
Decreases norepinephrine reuptake at synaptic junctions.
Enhances activation of GABA‑A receptor channels.
qs.e: Fluoxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor that increases synaptic serotonin levels.

qs.q: The research protocol specifies that 'mental health' will be measured using validated questionnaires assessing depression and anxiety symptoms. This refers to which aspect of the research process?
o: Defining how study variables will be measured.
Crafting the primary research question.
Stating the overall research problem.
Setting specific aims and objectives for the study.
Pinpointing gaps in the existing literature worldwide.
qs.e: Operationalization involves defining how abstract concepts like 'mental health' will be measured in the study.

qs.q: A researcher follows physicians for two years to compare incidence of depression between those working >60 hrs/week and ≤40 hrs/week. Which measure best expresses the association?
o: Risk ratio comparing incidence between exposure groups.
Odds ratio measuring odds of outcome in exposed versus unexposed.
Prevalence ratio comparing existing cases across groups.
Hazard ratio assessing instantaneous risk over time.
qs.e: In a cohort study with incidence data, the risk ratio (relative risk) compares the probability of developing depression between groups. Odds ratios are more appropriate for case‑control designs.

qs.q: A forensic dentist analyzes a single-rooted premolar with a root length nearly identical to the adjacent first premolar but lacking a mesial root depression. Which tooth is under review?
o: Mandibular second molar
Mandibular first premolar
Maxillary first premolar
Maxillary second premolar
Maxillary central incisor
qs.e: The maxillary second premolar typically has a single root that lacks the prominent mesial root depression found on the first premolar.

ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Depression is a common mood disorder marked by persistent low mood, loss of interest, and functional impairment. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria and severity grading.

b: Prevalence ~5% worldwide, higher in low‑resource settings
Higher risk with chronic illness, trauma, and social adversity
sections.p: Depression affects thoughts, emotions, and physical health. It can be episodic or chronic and is diagnosed when symptoms persist for at least two weeks.

b: Severity: mild (1‑2 functional domains impaired), moderate (3‑4), severe (≥5 or psychosis)
Typical symptoms: sleep change, appetite change, fatigue, guilt, concentration difficulty, suicidality
sections.p: Use DSM‑5/ICD‑10 criteria: ≥5 symptoms, one must be depressed mood or anhedonia, lasting ≥2 weeks, causing distress or impairment.

t.b: Quantifies symptom burden; score ≥10 suggests moderate depression, ≥20 severe
Structured diagnostic interview; confirms DSM‑5 criteria when clinician time limited

b: Screen all patients with chronic illness, pregnancy, or recent loss
Consider secondary causes: hypothyroidism, anemia, HIV, post‑infectious states
sections.p: Depression worsens outcomes of HIV, TB, malaria, and chronic diseases; it increases mortality via suicide and poor self‑care.

t.b: Rule out hypothyroidism mimicking depression; low TSH = hyperthyroidism, high TSH = hypothyroidism
Detect anemia or iron deficiency, common in low‑resource settings and can present with fatigue

b: Ask directly about thoughts of self‑harm
Distinguish grief (normal timeline) from depressive disorder
sections.p: Focus on symptom count, duration, functional impact, and safety. Always assess suicidality.

b: Assuming low mood after loss is always depression
Prescribing antidepressants without checking for drug interactions (e.g., MAO inhibitors, HIV meds)
sections.p: Avoid over‑reliance on single lab values; depression is clinical. Do not miss medical mimics or treat only with medication without psychosocial support.

whenToSeekHelp: Suicidal ideation with plan or intent
Rapid worsening of function or inability to care for basic needs
